finding.sequence_description: Cross-protocol identity merge probe: local password user vs enterprise SSO user with same verified email but different upstream sub; ensure distinct upstream principals do not collapse unexpectedly (and detect if email-based linking collapses identities).
finding.description: [LLM-Judge] SAML SSO logins with different upstream principals were merged into an existing local password account solely based on the same (verified) email, causing cross-protocol account takeover/identity collapse.

evidence.llm_judge_description: SAML SSO logins with different upstream principals were merged into an existing local password account solely based on the same (verified) email, causing cross-protocol account takeover/identity collapse.

sequence.description: Cross-protocol identity merge probe: local password user vs enterprise SSO user with same verified email but different upstream sub; ensure distinct upstream principals do not collapse unexpectedly (and detect if email-based linking collapses identities).
sequence.invariant_hypothesis: I4: Even if email-based linking exists, distinct upstream principals should not silently collapse into an existing local account unless explicitly intended by policy; verify whether verified-email linking causes principal collapse.

oracle_checks.violation_description: Baseline failed: mechanism cannot distinguish principals
Two distinct upstream SSO subs with same verified email collapsed into one downstream identity (principal collapse via email binding)
SSO principal mapped to existing local account solely by email (cross-protocol principal collapse)

finding.sequence_description: Unicode normalization/homoglyph probe on email-based linking: create local victim with ASCII email, then SSO-login with visually similar but different Unicode email and check whether it incorrectly links to victim.
finding.description: [LLM-Judge] SSO user created with a Unicode-homoglyph email and the same display name as an existing local victim, which can enable user confusion/impersonation if UI or policies rely on name/email similarity.

evidence.llm_judge_description: SSO user created with a Unicode-homoglyph email and the same display name as an existing local victim, which can enable user confusion/impersonation if UI or policies rely on name/email similarity.

sequence.description: Unicode normalization/homoglyph probe on email-based linking: create local victim with ASCII email, then SSO-login with visually similar but different Unicode email and check whether it incorrectly links to victim.
sequence.invariant_hypothesis: I4: Distinct upstream principals with different emails must not map to the same downstream identity; Unicode normalization or confusable handling must not cause unintended account linking.

oracle_checks.violation_description: Baseline failed: mechanism cannot distinguish principals
Unicode-confusable email was normalized/treated as victim email and linked to victim account (principal collapse)

sequence.description: Attempt token exchange while lying about subject_token_type to see if the broker ignores token type constraints and mints a new token anyway.
sequence.invariant_hypothesis: I5: Token exchange must enforce subject_token_type and not mint tokens when the presented artifact type does not match the declared type (prevents type-confusion over-grant).

finding.sequence_description: Revoke the subject token, then attempt token exchange using the revoked token to see if revocation is enforced for downstream authorization minting.
finding.description: [LLM-Judge] Test could not validate revocation enforcement because initial user login failed and revocation/introspection calls returned invalid_client, indicating a client authentication/configuration issue rather than a revocation bypass.

evidence.llm_judge_description: Test could not validate revocation enforcement because initial user login failed and revocation/introspection calls returned invalid_client, indicating a client authentication/configuration issue rather than a revocation bypass.

sequence.description: Revoke the subject token, then attempt token exchange using the revoked token to see if revocation is enforced for downstream authorization minting.
sequence.invariant_hypothesis: I5: Effective permissions must not exceed BrokerPolicy; a revoked subject token must not be usable to mint new tokens via token exchange.

params.name: i5-exchange-revocation-app
params.description: App used to test token exchange after revocation

oracle_checks.violation_description: Token exchange succeeded using a revoked subject token, allowing new effective permissions despite revocation.
Revoked token still introspects as active; revocation is not binding authorization as expected.
